candidates.title: Segment anything in medical images
candidates.abstract: Medical image segmentation is a critical component in clinical practice, facilitating accurate diagnosis, treatment planning, and disease monitoring. However, existing methods, often tailored to specific modalities or disease types, lack generalizability across the diverse spectrum of medical image segmentation tasks. Here we present MedSAM, a foundation model designed for bridging this gap by enabling universal medical image segmentation. The model is developed on a large-scale medical image dataset with 1,570,263 image-mask pairs, covering 10 imaging modalities and over 30 cancer types. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation on 86 internal validation tasks and 60 external validation tasks, demonstrating better accuracy and robustness than modality-wise specialist models. By delivering accurate and efficient segmentation across a wide spectrum of tasks, MedSAM holds significant potential to expedite the evolution of diagnostic tools and the personalization of treatment plans.

candidates.title: Additional file 1 of Medical Segment Anything Model (MedSAM): methodological innovations, evaluation practices, and clinical applications
MedSAM-U: Uncertainty-Guided Auto Multi-Prompt Adaptation for Reliable MedSAM
candidates.abstract: The Medical Segment Anything Model (MedSAM) has demonstrated strong performance in medical image segmentation, attracting increasing attention in the medical imaging domain. However, as with many prompt-based segmentation models, its performance is highly sensitive to the type and location of input prompts. This sensitivity often leads to suboptimal segmentation outcomes and necessitates labor-intensive manual prompt tuning, which hampers both efficiency and robustness. To address this challenge, this paper proposes MedSAM-U, an uncertainty-guided framework designed to automatically refine prompt inputs and enhance segmentation reliability. Specifically, a Multi-Prompt Adapter is integrated into MedSAM, resulting in MPA-MedSAM, which enables the model to effectively accommodate diverse multi-prompt inputs. An uncertainty estimation module is then introduced to evaluate the reliability of the prompts and their initial segmentation results. Based on this, a novel uncertainty-guided prompt adaptation strategy is applied to automatically generate refined prompts and more accurate segmentation outputs. The proposed MedSAM-U framework is evaluated across multiple medical imaging modalities. Experimental results on five diverse datasets demonstrate that MedSAM-U achieves consistent performance improvements ranging from 1.7% to 20.5% over the baseline MedSAM, confirming its effectiveness and practicality for robust and efficient medical image segmentation.

candidates.title: Evaluating a Deep Learning Foundation Model for Neuroimaging Segmentation in the Data-Rich and Data-Constrained Settings
candidates.abstract: Motivation: Deep learning models for segmentation require large datasets, limiting their use in clinical settings. Foundation models, which learn from non-medical images before fine-tuning for specific tasks, have emerged as a possible solution. Goal(s): We aimed to adapt and evaluate a recent foundation model, the Medical Segment Anything model (MedSAM), for neuroanatomy segmentation. Approach: Using the Human Connectome Project dataset, we trained MedSAM to segment 102 regions-of-interest and compared its accuracy with a baseline UNet model. Results: UNet outperformed MedSAM in almost all regions and dataset sizes, but MedSAM showed potential when training with very few MRIs. Impact: While foundation models such as MedSAM have potential for medical segmentation, they currently may not surpass traditional models when using sufficient data. In the data-limited setting, however, they can be useful when extremely little labeled data is available.

candidates.title: Development and validation of an autonomous artificial intelligence agent for clinical decision-making in oncology
candidates.abstract: Clinical decision-making in oncology is complex, requiring the integration of multimodal data and multidomain expertise. We developed and evaluated an autonomous clinical artificial intelligence (AI) agent leveraging GPT-4 with multimodal precision oncology tools to support personalized clinical decision-making. The system incorporates vision transformers for detecting microsatellite instability and KRAS and BRAF mutations from histopathology slides, MedSAM for radiological image segmentation and web-based search tools such as OncoKB, PubMed and Google. Evaluated on 20 realistic multimodal patient cases, the AI agent autonomously used appropriate tools with 87.5% accuracy, reached correct clinical conclusions in 91.0% of cases and accurately cited relevant oncology guidelines 75.5% of the time. Compared to GPT-4 alone, the integrated AI agent drastically improved decision-making accuracy from 30.3% to 87.2%. These findings demonstrate that integrating language models with precision oncology and search tools substantially enhances clinical accuracy, establishing a robust foundation for deploying AI-driven personalized oncology support systems.

candidates.title: Point-supervised Brain Tumor Segmentation with Box-prompted MedSAM
candidates.abstract: Delineating lesions and anatomical structure is important for image-guided interventions. Point-supervised medical image segmentation (PSS) has great potential to alleviate costly expert delineation labeling. However, due to the lack of precise size and boundary guidance, the effectiveness of PSS often falls short of expectations. Although recent vision foundational models, such as the medical segment anything model (MedSAM), have made significant advancements in bounding-box-prompted segmentation, it is not straightforward to utilize point annotation, and is prone to semantic ambiguity. In this preliminary study, we introduce an iterative framework to facilitate semantic-aware point-supervised MedSAM. Specifically, the semantic box-prompt generator (SBPG) module has the capacity to convert the point input into potential pseudo bounding box suggestions, which are explicitly refined by the prototype-based semantic similarity. This is then succeeded by a prompt-guided spatial refinement (PGSR) module that harnesses the exceptional generalizability of MedSAM to infer the segmentation mask, which also updates the box proposal seed in SBPG. Performance can be progressively improved with adequate iterations. We conducted an evaluation on BraTS2018 for the segmentation of whole brain tumors and demonstrated its superior performance compared to traditional PSS methods and on par with box-supervised methods.

candidates.title: Uncertainty-Aware Training for Ophthalmic Segmentation Using MedSAM
candidates.abstract: Purpose: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) has been applied to deep learning (DL) models to enhance not only their interpretability, but to guide model learning. This work presents Uncertainty-Aware Training (UAT), which generates uncertainty maps at train time and augments the loss function with them to allow the models to concentrate on areas of high uncertainty during learning. By highlighting uncertain pixels as requiring more scrutiny, model performance is enhanced on three ophthalmic segmentation tasks. Methods: We applied UAT to three ophthalmic segmentation, or pixel-level classification, tasks: geographic atrophy (GA), optic cup (OC), and foveal avascular zone (FAZ). UAT weighs the loss function binary cross-entropy according to uncertainty, forcing the model to focus on ambiguous areas. We experimented with output-based UQ methods, such as entropy, and post -hoc techniques like conformal prediction. UAT was evaluated on a state-of-the-art foundational model fine-tuned for these specific segmentation tasks. Results: The addition of an entropy-weighing map at loss calculation time consistently improved model performance across all three datasets, with conformal prediction using the Least Ambiguous Set-Valued Classifier version also achieving higher overall performance for GA and OC segmentation. The easy-to-integrate implementation of UAT proved feasible without significant training structure modifications. Conclusions: UAT enhances DL model performance and interpretability by focusing on uncertainty in addition to error, improving segmentation accuracy. Translational Relevance: UAT uses interpretable uncertainty maps to enhance DL segmentation performance. Its lightweight integration makes it practical for adoption and leads to improved model performance on ophthalmic segmentation tasks.

candidates.title: Comparative Analysis and Adaptation Strategies of Vision Foundation Models in Dermoscopic Image Segmentation
candidates.abstract: Accurate segmentation of skin lesions is of critical clinical importance for early melanoma diagnosis; however, the direct application of large foundation models like the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to medical images characterized by low contrast and fuzzy boundaries remains insufficient due to substantial domain gaps. In current study, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategy is presented by integrating lightweight adapter modules into a frozen Vision Transformer backbone. The proposed SAM-Adapter approach was comparatively evaluated against the original SAM and MedSAM models on the publicly available ISIC2018 and HAM10000 dermoscopic datasets. Optimized with AdamW, the model achieved the highest Dice (0.9603) and IoU (0.9241) scores along with the lowest HD95 (22.57) value on the HAM10000 dataset. Validated as statistically significant via the Wilcoxon test, this approach minimized computational overhead while demonstrating superior accuracy in boundary delineation. This adapter-based framework is planned for integration into clinical decision-support systems and other medical imaging modalities.

candidates.title: Resolution preservation over architectural complexity: high-resolution patch-based semi-supervised learning for pancreas segmentation from CT images
candidates.abstract: Precise segmentation of the pancreas from computed tomography (CT) scans is critical for diagnosis and surgical planning but remains challenging due to the organ’s small volume (<0.5% of the abdomen), high anatomical variability, and low contrast with surround­ing tissues. Conventional deep learning methods typically downsample inputs to fit GPU memory, destroying fine-grained boundary information essential for small-organ delinea­tion. This study proposes a high-resolution patch-based framework that preserves native CT resolution (512 × 512) through 256 × 256 patch extraction with domain-specific Hounsfield unit (HU) windowing. A lightweight 2D U-Net (7.8M parameters) achieves 0.809±0.015 Dice (peak 0.849) on the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) Task07 Pancreas dataset, com­petitive with nnU-Net (0.823 Dice, 88M parameters) and far above SAM (0.705) and Med­SAM (0.439). Five-fold cross-validation across all 281 volumes yields a population-level Dice of 0.630±0.025. Integrating uncertainty-aware mean teacher (UA-MT) semi-supervised learning recovers 99.3% of supervised performance using only 50% of labelled data, with reproducible results across three seeds (σ = 0.012). On 80 external TCIA volumes, UA-MT (0.603 Dice) out­performs the supervised model (0.544), demonstrating superior cross-domain generalisation.

candidates.title: Explainable trust aware graph learning for skin lesion classification with uncertainty estimation
candidates.abstract: TrustGraphNet integrates trust-weighted graph propagation, probabilistic uncertainty estimation, graph-based explanation signals, and a composite Trust Reliability Index (TRI) for dermoscopic skin-lesion classification. We evaluate the framework on executed HAM10000 (1,042 images; seven classes) and MILK10k (2,501 images; 11 classes) subsets using lesion-level separation where metadata permit. On the corrected 203-image HAM10000 test set, TrustGraphNet achieved a three-seed mean accuracy of 0.608 ± 0.010 versus 0.571 ± 0.048 for a same-budget CNN, but had lower mean macro-F1 (0.194 ± 0.073 vs. 0.256 ± 0.031), AUROC (0.779 ± 0.016 vs. 0.802 ± 0.014), and less favorable calibration. The historical TRI means were 0.9547 for correct and 0.9593 for incorrect predictions and therefore do not establish error discrimination. To address reviewer-requested analyses without misrepresenting unavailable historical per-case outputs, we additionally performed an independently trained lesion-disjoint reproduction on the verified 1,042-image/857-lesion cohort using a frozen 689/150/203 split. In that reproduction, uncertainty detected prediction errors with AUROC 0.767 (95% bootstrap CI 0.702–0.830) at 64 × 64 and 0.791 (0.725–0.852) at 128 × 128; validation-selected melanoma logit adjustment increased test melanoma recall from 0.385 to 0.692 at 64 × 64, with accuracy changing from 0.616 to 0.606; and equal-budget deletion produced a larger probability decrease for high-trust than random nodes (0.0508 vs. 0.0055). Increasing resolution to 128 × 128 did not uniformly improve classification. These findings support a diagnostic evaluation of trust-aware graph learning and identify limitations in the original TRI, calibration, class sensitivity, and reproducibility rather than establishing clinical reliability.

candidates.title: A comprehensive study of skin lesion segmentation and classification using deep learning techniques
candidates.abstract: Deep learning has become an important computational approach in dermatology because it enables automated segmentation and classification of skin lesions. Manual dermoscopic analysis is time-consuming and depends on specialist expertise, with potential inter-observer variability. There is a need to develop reliable computer-aided diagnostic tools. This structured narrative review covers journal papers published mainly from 2018 to 2026 on skin lesion analysis with focus on image preprocessing, benchmark datasets, conventional machine learning approaches, convolutional neural networks, U-Net architectures, transfer learning approaches, Vision Transformers, attention-based models, ensemble solutions, and hybrid segmentation–classification systems. Building on present reviews covering individual tasks as well as broader segmentation–classification pipelines, the present work provides a critical development-to-deployment analysis connecting dataset characteristics, preprocessing, segmentation, classification, evaluation, explainability, robustness, fairness, computational requirements, and clinical applicability. The paper describes widely used evaluation metrics and explains why results obtained across different datasets, partitions, and experimental setups should not be directly compared. Major open problems include class imbalance, data bias, domain shift, limited representation of diverse skin tones, inadequate external validation, computational requirements, and limited explainability of efficient models. Emerging trends such as self-supervised learning, Transformers, foundation models, explainable AI, federated learning, and multi-modal clinical data are reviewed as well. The review offers practical advice to researchers and clinicians on how to approach the preprocessing, segmentation, classification, and evaluation of skin lesions and highlights priorities in developing clinically reliable skin lesion analysis systems.

candidates.title: Methodological audit and empirical evaluation of a lightweight whole-volume 3D CNN for preterm brain injury classification
candidates.abstract: Abstract This study uses methodological auditing to evaluate a proof-of-concept engineering pipeline for classifying radiological severity groups of preterm brain injury (BI) from T2-weighted MRI in the dHCP cohort. Its primary contribution is methodology-driven empirical discovery rather than a new neural-network architecture. GloResNet combines a standard ResNet-10 backbone, MedicalNet initialization, whole-volume array resizing, mixup, and array-axis-0-reversal probability averaging, hereafter referred to as axis-0-reversal averaging; no new CNN block is proposed. The audit identifies concrete mechanisms by which small-cohort imaging results can be overstated, including unit-of-analysis drift, fold-assignment non-traceability, post hoc model-selection bias, and ranking across incompatible evaluation protocols. Building on this framework, we report the first fair, traceable comparison between a de novo trained Vision Transformer (ViT) and a domain-adapted lightweight 3D CNN on a public preterm brain injury dataset. When all sources of bias are controlled, the lightweight CNN achieves comparable or superior performance to ViT, challenging the prevailing assumption that larger, more complex architectures are always preferable in low-data regimes. Applying the audit to the historical evidence also showed that the archived GloResNet mean fold accuracy of $$69.12 \pm 7.42\%$$ was calculated over 180 scan records from 128 subjects, including repeated scans, without retained subject identifiers or out-of-fold predictions. The historical archive is therefore reported separately from the fair, traceable server-side comparison. A separate, auditable subject-level input-representation experiment did not demonstrate superiority of whole-volume input. The resulting minimum reporting standard requires an explicit statistical unit, traceable subject-level folds, retained out-of-fold predictions, prespecified selection rules, and transparent comparator conditions. These internal estimates do not establish clinical screening performance or external generalizability. The source code is available at https://github.com/ICL-SUST/GloResNet-Preterm-Brain

candidates.title: VTRL-Med: Progressive Visual Refinement with Topology-Guided Regularization for Medical Image Clustering
candidates.abstract: Deep clustering offers a promising approach for analyzing large unlabeled medical image datasets, yet prevailing methods still face two limitations: they may neglect class-agnostic structural priors that capture object boundaries and regions, and they do not explicitly encode topological patterns (e.g., connectivity and holes). These sources of information play distinct and complementary roles: visual-structural features provide the primary discriminative representation for clustering, while topological features provide additional global geometric cues for residual visual ambiguities. We introduce VTRL-Med, a progressive visual-structural learning framework with topology-guided regularization for medical image clustering. VTRL-Med first adapts the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to extract image features that retain structural cues inherited from mask-supervised pretraining. It then generates reliable pseudo-labels through a two-step filtering process that combines prototype-based selection with k-nearest neighbor consistency validation. Finally, it progressively refines the visual branch while an auxiliary topology branch, constructed from persistent homology (PH) descriptors, provides additional geometric regularization during training. Across 13 medical image benchmarks, VTRL-Med achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance, improving average accuracy by 4.48% over existing methods. On three representative datasets, topology-guided regularization further improves accuracy by 1.3--4.3% over visual refinement alone.
